target_audience: University students (Computer Science or Cybersecurity) and Tech Enthusiasts

outline.target_audience: University students (Computer Science or Cybersecurity) and Tech Enthusiasts

sections.title: The Tracing Dilemma
sections.content: Introduction to the conflict between public health (tracking virus spread) and individual privacy (data security). Explain why centralized databases are risky (potential for government surveillance).
sections.example: Imagine Alice and Bob are in a park. If Bob gets sick later, how can Alice be notified without a central server knowing exactly where they were or who they are?

sections.title: Prerequisite: The One-Way Hash & Bluetooth RSSI
sections.content: Briefly explain Cryptographic Hash Functions (generating a unique digital fingerprint that can't be reversed) and Bluetooth Low Energy (using signal strength/RSSI to estimate distance between devices).
sections.example: Visual: A meat grinder icon. Put in a secret word (Input), get out a random string (Hash). You can't turn the string back into the word.

sections.title: Phase 1: Generating Ephemeral IDs (The Nicknames)
sections.content: Each phone generates a rotating Secret Key daily. From this, it derives 'Ephemeral IDs' (EphIDs) that change every 15 minutes using a hash function. This prevents 'stalking' because the ID is constantly changing.
sections.example: Alice's phone creates a daily secret 'Sunlight'. Every 15 mins, it calculates Hash('Sunlight' + Time) to create IDs like 'A1x9', then 'B2z8'. She broadcasts these 'nicknames' via Bluetooth.

sections.title: Phase 2: The Digital Handshake
sections.content: When two phones are close, they exchange and store these EphIDs locally on the device (not a server). This is the 'Decentralized' part—the 'diary' of contacts stays on the phone.
sections.example: Alice and Bob sit on a bench. Alice's phone hears 'B2z8' and writes it in a private digital diary. Bob's phone hears 'A1x9' and does the same. Neither knows the other's real identity.

sections.title: Phase 3: Exposure Notification (The Bulletin Board)
sections.content: If Bob tests positive, he uploads his 'Secret Key' (not his location or contact list) to a public server. Everyone else's phone downloads the list of 'Infected Keys' and reconstructs the EphIDs to see if any match their local diary.
sections.example: Bob uploads his key 'Moonlight'. Alice's phone downloads it, calculates all possible IDs 'Moonlight' would have produced, and sees 'B2z8' matches an entry in her diary. Her phone alerts her: 'Potential Exposure!'

sections.title: Summary & Privacy Benefits
sections.content: Recap the flow: Local Generation -> Local Storage -> Voluntary Disclosure -> Local Matching. Emphasize that the server never knows 'who met whom' or 'where'.
sections.example: Comparison Chart: Centralized (Server knows all) vs. DP-3T (Server is just a bulletin board, intelligence stays at the edge/phones).

storyboard.title: The Tracing Dilemma
lecture_lines: Digital contact tracing helps stop virus spread quickly.
But centralized databases risk mass government surveillance.
Can we trace contacts without knowing locations or identities?
animations: Show a grid of person icons. Gradually turn some icons red (#e74c3c) to represent virus spread.
Transition to a central 'Big Brother' server icon collecting lines from all icons. Add a red 'Surveillance' label.
Remove the server. Show Alice and Bob icons with a distance line between them. A 'Privacy-First' shield (#2ecc71) appears.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: The One-Way Hash & Bluetooth RSSI
lecture_lines: Cryptographic hashes create unique, irreversible digital fingerprints.
Bluetooth RSSI measures signal strength to estimate distance.
These tools enable privacy-preserving proximity detection.
animations: A 'Input' box takes in 'Data'. It passes through a 'Hash Function' gear (#95a5a6) and produces a hex string 'a7b2...'.
Attempt to reverse the 'a7b2...' string through the gear. The gear turns red (#e74c3c) and a 'No Entry' sign appears.
Two phone icons with expanding blue rings (#3498db). A label shows 'RSSI' decreasing as distance increases.

storyboard.title: Phase 1: Generating Ephemeral IDs (The Nicknames)
lecture_lines: Each phone generates a secret daily key locally.
Every 15 minutes, it derives a new Ephemeral ID.
Hashing the secret key ensures IDs are unlinkable.
Alice broadcasts these rotating nicknames via Bluetooth.
Frequent rotation prevents long-term tracking of individuals.
animations: Display a 'Secret Key' box (#3498db) inside a phone.
A clock icon rotates. A timer increments from 00:00 to 00:15.
The 'Secret Key' and 'Time' merge into a 'Hash' box (#2ecc71).
Out of the 'Hash' box comes 'EphID_1' (#f1c40f). It replaces the previous ID.
The 'EphID_1' label pulses and broadcasts outward-moving arcs to simulate Bluetooth signal.

storyboard.title: Phase 2: The Digital Handshake
lecture_lines: Phones exchange these nicknames when they are close.
Each device stores received IDs in a local diary.
No central server knows who Alice and Bob are.
animations: Place Alice and Bob icons on left/right. Each has a phone.
A small packet labeled 'EphID_A' moves from Alice to Bob.
A small packet labeled 'EphID_B' moves from Bob to Alice.
Zoom into Alice's phone. A list titled 'Contact Diary' scrolls up, adding 'EphID_B' to the bottom row.
Zoom into Bob's phone. A similar 'Contact Diary' adds 'EphID_A'. Both phones remain disconnected from any server.

storyboard.title: Phase 3: Exposure Notification (The Bulletin Board)
lecture_lines: If Bob tests positive, he uploads his daily key.
The central server acts as a public bulletin board.
Others download the keys and reconstruct potential IDs.
Alice's phone matches downloaded IDs against her local diary.
Matching IDs trigger a private local exposure alert.
animations: Bob's icon turns red (#e74c3c). An arrow sends his 'Daily Key' (#3498db) to a central 'Public Server' icon.
Alice's phone draws a 'Download' arrow from the Public Server, receiving the 'Daily Key'.
Inside Alice's phone, the 'Daily Key' is hashed with various times to create a set of 'Possible IDs' (#f1c40f).
A comparison animation: 'Possible IDs' side-by-side with 'Local Diary'. 'EphID_B' highlights in both.
A red warning banner (#e74c3c) 'Exposure Detected!' flashes on Alice's screen.

storyboard.title: Summary & Privacy Benefits
lecture_lines: DP-3T keeps data local and identities anonymous.
The server never learns location or social graphs.
Privacy and public health can coexist through decentralization.
animations: Display a split screen: 'Centralized' (lines to a cloud) vs 'DP-3T' (lines only between phones).
The 'Public Server' in DP-3T is highlighted as a 'Bulletin Board' that holds no personal data.
Final visual: Three icons - 'Key Generation', 'Local Storage', and 'Local Matching' - all within a 'Privacy Shield' (#2ecc71).
